cards.title: Running out of addresses
cards.text: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, which allows about 4.3 billion addresses — fewer than the number of connected devices today. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

cards.title: Three-way handshake
cards.text: TCP sets up a connection with three packets: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client answers ACK. Only then does data flow.

cards.question: Which protocol turns a domain name like example.com into an IP address?
On a local network, which protocol finds the MAC address for an IPv4 address?
Which protocol does the ping tool use?
cards.explanation: ping sends ICMP Echo Request messages and waits for Echo Replies.

cards.question: How many usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /24 subnet?
cards.explanation: 8 host bits give 256 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses.

cards.statement: UDP guarantees that packets arrive in the order they were sent.
cards.explanation: UDP makes no promises about order or delivery; TCP is the one that reorders and retransmits.

cards.statement: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP rather than TCP.
cards.explanation: QUIC implements reliability and encryption itself on top of UDP, avoiding TCP head-of-line blocking.

cards.note: Port 21 carries FTP's control connection; data uses separate connections.
Port 25 is server-to-server mail relay; mail clients usually submit on 587.
Most lookups use UDP; large responses and zone transfers use TCP.

cards.explanation: Hubs repeat raw signals, switches forward by MAC address, routers forward by IP address.
